question: What is the difference between `explicit` and implicit constructors?

scenes.sub: Should your constructor double as a silent type conversion?
scenes.say: explicit versus implicit constructors. A constructor that takes one argument is secretly also a type conversion, unless you say otherwise. Let's see the surprise.

scenes.head: Implicit: a silent conversion
scenes.say: Array has a constructor taking an int size. Without the keyword explicit, the compiler may use it to convert an int into an Array whenever it needs one. So print of ten compiles. The compiler quietly builds a temporary array of size ten and prints that, which is almost certainly not what the caller meant. Array a equals five compiles too.

scenes.head: explicit: conversions must be spelled out
scenes.say: Mark it explicit, and both lines fail to compile. explicit means this constructor can only be called when you name the type yourself. Direct initialization, with parentheses or braces, still works, and so does writing Array of ten on purpose. The conversion is still available. It just has to be visible in the code.

scenes.head: You already use both

panels.code:
std::string s = "hi";              // implicit: from const char*
std::vector<int> v = 10;           // explicit vector(size)
std::unique_ptr<int> p = new int;  // explicit: ownership

struct Point { explicit Point(int, int); };
Point q = {1, 2};                  // explicit blocks this too

scenes.say: The standard library uses both. A string from a literal is implicit, because that conversion is natural. A vector from an int is explicit, so a size is never mistaken for a value. unique p t r from a raw pointer is explicit, so taking ownership is always visible. And explicit matters with several arguments too: it blocks copy list initialization with equals braces. Conversion operators can be explicit as well, like explicit operator bool.

scenes.head: Side by side
scenes.say: Copy initialization with equals: only implicit compiles. Direct initialization: both work. Passing an int where an Array is expected: implicit converts silently, explicit refuses. Use implicit only when the conversion is natural and lossless, like string from a literal. Otherwise, make single argument constructors explicit by default.

lines: Implicit constructors double as silent type conversions.
explicit: only called when you name the type, e.g. Array(10).
Make single-argument constructors explicit unless the conversion is natural.
scenes.say: An implicit constructor doubles as a silent type conversion. An explicit one is only called when you name the type. Rule of thumb: make single argument constructors explicit, unless the conversion is truly natural.
